videos.script: IPsec lives in the network layer. It needs its own protocol numbers and its own ports, open on every firewall in the way. {{ipsec}} There is another way to build a VPN. Take the TLS that already protects every web page, and let it set up the tunnel. {{tls}} OpenVPN works like that. You will read its two configuration files, and watch its TLS handshake cross the ISP's router. {{handshake}} Both sides check a certificate. Then a second channel carries the traffic, with keys that came out of the handshake. {{channels}} Next comes a home router that lets almost nothing out. Over UDP, the tunnel never starts. Over TCP port 443, the port every web page uses, it is up within a second. {{port}} That trick has a price. A tunnel over TCP suffers badly when the network loses packets, and you will see why. {{cost}} The last part moves down a layer. Instead of joining two networks, you will stretch one Ethernet segment between the offices with VXLAN. {{vxlan}} An ARP broadcast sent at one office will be answered from the other. You will count the fifty bytes that costs, and learn when stretching a network is a mistake. {{stretch}}
